prose.def: A title for God meaning "the one who is, and who was, and who is coming" — the eternal one spanning all time.
prose.article: This isn't a single word but a fixed phrase used as a divine title, stitching together "the one being" (present participle of εἰμί), "the one who was" (its imperfect), and "the one coming" (present participle of ἔρχομαι). Strong's frames it as a name for the Eternal, applied as an epithet of Christ. The construction is striking because it freezes verb forms into noun-like titles, treating God's existence across past, present, and future as a name rather than a description.
prose.caution: There are no measured occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament corpus, and the lexical evidence cited (Abbott-Smith) covers only the ordinary verb "to be," not this phrase as a whole, so its sense rests on the construction itself rather than corpus measurement.

The Septuagint uses it twice to render Hebrew terms for snaring or being caught, and Moulton-Milligan note a striking parallel in the Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs, where someone looks for a way 'to trap me' — confirming this was ordinary Koine vocabulary for laying a snare.

prose.def: A trap or snare for catching prey, used figuratively for a hidden danger or temptation that suddenly catches someone.

The Byzantine NT has it 5 times, and although the rendering tool lists "dwell" and "become" as separate senses, those reflect how surrounding phrases were translated rather than different meanings of the word itself; the core sense throughout is "snare." It's heavily attested in the Septuagint (51 times), most often translating the Hebrew פָּח (a fowler's trap, 13 times), and it even turns up in a fifth-century Christian epitaph where the deceased boasts of escaping "the grievous nets and mournful snares of sin."

prose.def: A young boy or lad, originally a diminutive form but sometimes used more loosely for older youths.
